senses: Produced by the earth.
The thin, horny, transparent plate covering the upper surface of the end of a toe.
A small wading bird, Calidris alpina, found along the coast and having a distinctive black belly patch in its breeding plumage. A type of stint.
A test for the presence of a substance using the reaction of an antibody to its antigen, making use of the high selectivity of components of biological immune systems.
examples: An over-the-counter, pee-on-a-stick pregnancy test is an immunoassay.

senses: To appear magically; to teleport to or from a place.
ety: From Late Latin apparēre (“to appear”), as of a servant who appears on being summoned. A back-formation from apparition.
examples: What had silenced her, however, was the enormous demonic object that had apparated in the air beyond the tunnel's exit.

senses: A stubble field left unploughed until late in the autumn, so that it can be cropped by cattle.
ety: From Middle English rewayn, from Anglo-Norman rewain, from an Old Northern French variant of Old French regain (“an increase”), from re- + gaigner (“to till, win”). The alternative forms represent replacement of unanalysable final /ən/ with the more tractable suffixes -et, -ing; roughing presumably relies on a lost pronunciation of rough as /ˈɹaʊ/.

senses: Any snake in the family Colubridae, completely covered in scales and mostly nonvenomous.
ety: From translingual Colubridae, from the genus translingual Coluber, from Latin coluber (“snake”).

senses: A video and/or audio broadcast transmitted via the Internet
A bicycle lane or path.
The top or superior part of a thing.
The council or ruling body of the University of Cambridge prior to the constitution of 1856.
ety: Learned borrowing from Latin caput (“the head”). Doublet of cape, capo, chef, and chief, and distantly of head and Howth.

senses: Resembling or relating to podzol.
A person who winnows.
A form of fan or basket used for winnowing.
One who evacuates; a nullifier.
An agent for emptying, especially an instrument for removing fragments of stone from the bladder after litholapaxy.
A person who creates forgeries, falsifies documents with intent to defraud, e.g. to create a false will or illicit copies of currency; counterfeiter.
A person who forges metals.
ety: From Middle English forger, forgere, from Old French forgiere; equivalent to forge + -er.

senses: a male blues musician
A Eurasian sparrowhawk, Accipiter nisus, a small, short-winged European hawk that preys on smaller birds.
A female such bird, a male being a musket.
ety: From Middle English sparhauk, sperhauk, from Old English spearhafoc, spearhabuc (“sparrow-hawk”), from Proto-West Germanic *sparwahabuk, from Proto-Germanic *sparwahabukaz, equivalent to sparrow + hawk. Cognate with Danish spurvehøg (“sparrowhawk”), Swedish sparvhök (“sparrowhawk”), Icelandic sparrhaukur (“sparrowhawk”).

senses: Impossible to resolve; insoluble.
Impossible to separate into its component parts.
A percussive note in which the drumstick hits both the head and the rim of the drum.
A percussive sting or flourish used to punctuate a joke in a cabaret or vaudeville act.
A barb or pap under the tongue of a cow or horse.
ety: From Middle English barbel, from Old French barbel, from Vulgar Latin *barbellus, from Late Latin barbulus, diminutive of Latin barbus (“barbel”); barbus itself is from barba (“beard”). By surface analysis, Latin barb(us) (“beard, barbel”) + -el (diminutive suffix), and also, by surface analysis, barb (“sharp, extruding structure”) + -el (diminutive suffix).

senses: A robot that is designed to look and act like a human.
examples: Originally he'd entered the Game to rescue the others. He was a sanitation Mechanoid, programmed to clean, and, in theory, should have been immune to the Game's lure. But he wasn't.

senses: Resembling a lobe.
ety: From Latin lobātus, equivalent to lobe + -ate.

senses: The process by which a single vowel sound (monophthong) shifts to a two-vowel vocalization (diphthong).
Like a hare.
A shout of "brava!".
ety: From Italian brava, feminine of bravo.

senses: A traditional Hungarian fruit brandy.
examples: An apricot palinka made with honey, apricot juice and lime — every bit as captivating as the new food in town.

senses: The amount that can be moved at once with a shovel.
examples: One shovelful of dirt makes a molehill; a million shovelfuls make a mountain.
Two workers each had a shovelful of snow. There were two shovelsful of snow.
The doors are at the right level for firing, which normally is down one side of the firebox at a time, unlike our own practice, which is to fire each side of the firebox with alternate shovelfuls.

senses: A small deep-fried cornmeal cake.
ety: Perhaps because they were once thrown to hungry dogs to quieten them.

senses: To regard something as ideal.
To conceive or form an ideal.
To portray using idealization.
Synonym of freeze pop, flavoured ice or frozen fruit juice in a tube.
Cartilage; now especially: cartilage present, as a tough substance, in meat.
Bone not yet hardened by age and hard work.
ety: From Middle English gristel, grystyl, from Old English gristel (“gristle, cartilage”), Proto-West Germanic *gristl, of obscure origin; possibly from a pre-Germanic substrate language. Seemingly equivalent to a diminutive of Old English grist (“a grinding”), equivalent to modern English grist + -le; possibly related to Proto-Germanic *gredaną (“to crunch”). Cognate with Old Frisian gristel, gerstel (“gristle, cartilage”), Middle Low German gristel (“gristle”).

senses: A machine that packages tea into teabags.
examples: The equipment used, adapted from a Pneumatic Scale Co. teabagger, is a high-speed, horizontal form-fill-seal machine. The web is filled with ground coffee, over-packaged and at the same time flushed with an inert gas.

senses: A unit of volume equivalent to eight chupas.
ety: From Spanish ganta, from Cebuano gantang, from Malay gantang. Doublet of gantang.

senses: UK standard spelling of draftsmanship.
A traditional Irish potato pancake.
Love, fondness.
ety: From an expressively lengthened pronunciation of love ([lʌːv]~[lɜːv]~[lɐːv]). The spelling is based on non-rhotic English.

senses: A network or group of people who are somehow affiliated or linked spiritually.
ety: Coined by American writer Kurt Vonnegut in 1963, in the novel Cat's Cradle.
examples: I do want to go to Arlinghurst, even though it's moronic and awful and there's no privacy at all, because I have started to build my karass there. I have the book club,I have the library—both libraries.

senses: To make a verbal claim to.
ety: Respelling and grammatical repurposing of bags I, as used to claim something for oneself, for example, Bags I have the top bunk!.
examples: I bagsy the top bunk of the bed.

senses: Resembling a weasel (in appearance).
Devious; cunning; misleading; sneaky.
examples: At three minutes past six the door opened to admit the naked, scrawny figure of Tingaling Bell. He had a sharp weasely face and a miserable body on which each bone showed.
On still weasellier, greasier members of the clique.
I lifted the extension, slowly released the button, easing in mid-ring like the weaselliest weasel.

senses: A tool used to bore through rock when sinking shafts.
ety: Borrowed into Middle English from Old French trepan, from Latin trepanum, from Ancient Greek τρύπανον (trúpanon, “auger, borer”). Doublet of trephine.

senses: A male saxophonist.
